```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(comment = NA)
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))
bca <- read_rds("data/bca262.rds")
```

## AI writes the first draft; you own the result

- AI tools are allowed for the research project, with attribution. They are not allowed in exams.
- AI is good at R syntax. It does not know your data.
- You are responsible for every number on your slides, whoever typed the code.

::: {.key-point}
Your job shifts from writing code to checking it.
:::

## Will you notice if the AI is wrong?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Visible errors**

- The code stops with an error.
- The chart looks obviously wrong.

Ask the AI again.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Silent errors**

- The code runs and the chart looks fine.
- The numbers are wrong.

You must catch these yourself.
:::
::::

::: {.warning}
Common silent errors: a median that mixes property types, a join that duplicates rows, a wrong census vector, a geocoding match in the wrong city.
:::

## Two kinds of AI tools

- **Coding agents in Positron or the Terminal.** They read the files in your `c407` folder, write code, and run it. You need one from deck 08 on.
- **Chat tools in a browser.** They see only what you paste: your question, code, and output.

The same checks apply to both.

## Install a coding agent in Positron

1. Open the **c407 folder** as your workspace.
2. Open the **Extensions** view: **Ctrl+Shift+X** on Windows, **Cmd+Shift+X** on macOS.
3. Search for **Codex** or **Claude Code**, and click **Install**.
4. Open the agent's panel and sign in with your ChatGPT or Claude account.

Signing in with an account needs no API key. Each tool needs a plan that includes it.

::: {.warning}
Check the publisher before you install: **OpenAI** for Codex, **Anthropic** for Claude Code. Lookalike extensions exist.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Positron installs extensions from Open VSX, not the VS Code Marketplace.
- If the extension does not appear, install the agent's command-line version and run it in Positron's Terminal.
:::

## AGENTS.md gives the agent the course rules

- `AGENTS.md` in your `c407` folder lists where files go, which packages to use, and the data traps in this course.
- Codex reads it automatically. Claude Code reads it through `CLAUDE.md`, which is also in your folder.
- You don't need to repeat these rules in your requests.

## Tell the agent the goal and the file

::: {.small}
```text
In a new Quarto document, chart the median sale price by year
in the City of Vancouver from data/bca262.rds,
separately for single-family and strata homes.
```
:::

- The agent runs `glimpse()` on the data and reads `AGENTS.md` itself. You paste neither.
- State the choices you have already made: the place, the years, the property types.

::: {.key-point}
The agent knows R. Only you know what you want to measure.
:::

## Manage the conversation

Each new message is processed together with the whole conversation so far. Long conversations use up your plan's limit faster, and the answers can get worse: the AI loses early instructions and mixes in old versions of your code.

- Use one conversation per task. Start a new one when the topic changes.
- When answers get worse, ask for a short summary and paste it into a new conversation.
- Point the agent to files instead of pasting their contents.

## If you use a chat tool

A chat tool sees only what you paste, so paste what an agent would read for itself:

::: {.small}
```text
I'm using R and the tidyverse in a Quarto document.
<paste the "COMM 407 Course Rules" section of AGENTS.md>
`bca` holds BC Assessment sales. Here is glimpse(bca): <paste output>

Goal: the median sale price by year in the City of Vancouver,
separately for single-family and strata homes.
```
:::

- Paste `glimpse()` or `head()` output, never whole tables.
- To fix an error, paste only the error and the code that caused it.

## Demo: how have Vancouver prices changed?

::: {.small}
```text
How have home prices in the City of Vancouver changed since 2000?
Make a chart of the median sale price by year from data/bca262.rds,
in a new Quarto document.
```
:::

The agent's code, shortened:

```{r}
#| label: demo-code
van <- bca |> filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver")

by_year <- van |>
  group_by(sale_year = year(sale_date)) |>
  summarise(median_price = median(price))
```

## The agent's summary

```{r}
#| label: demo-chart
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.4
ggplot(by_year, aes(sale_year, median_price)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar())
```

::: {.small}
> The rise was uneven. It was fast in 2004–2007 and 2020–2024, and nearly flat in 2011–2015 and 2017–2019.
>
> I included all sales, both houses ("S/F Res") and strata units like condos ("Strata Res"). The median mixes the two, so part of any change could come from a shift in which type sells.
:::

Were prices nearly flat from 2011 to 2015?

::: {.notes}
- Tested on 2026-10-18 with Claude Sonnet in a fresh copy of the student `c407` folder, so `AGENTS.md` was loaded. The quotes are its own words. It also filtered on `juris_label`, not the wider `aa_label`, and flagged 2026 as a partial year.
- A live run will differ. If the agent splits by type on its own, ask the class what the single line would have told them.
- Two other prompts came out right: sales per year (the agent dropped the partial 2026 and said why) and price per square foot of houses (it dropped sales without a floor area and said how many). Mechanical slips are now rare; choices like this one remain.
:::

## Split by property type before you trust a trend

```{r}
#| label: demo-split
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.2
by_type <- van |>
  group_by(act_use_cat, sale_year = year(sale_date)) |>
  summarise(median_price = median(price), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(by_type, aes(sale_year, median_price, colour = act_use_cat)) +
  geom_line()
```

## Both types rose; the mix hid it

::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: demo-mix
mix <- van |>
  filter(year(sale_date) %in% c(2011, 2015)) |>
  group_by(sale_year = year(sale_date)) |>
  summarise(single_family = median(price[act_use_cat == "S/F Res"]),
            strata = median(price[act_use_cat == "Strata Res"]),
            all_sales = median(price),
            strata_share = mean(act_use_cat == "Strata Res"))
mix
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: demo-pct
#| include: false
pct <- function(x) round(100 * (x[2] / x[1] - 1))
```

Single-family prices rose `r pct(mix$single_family)`% and strata prices `r pct(mix$strata)`%, yet the median of all sales rose only `r pct(mix$all_sales)`%. Cheaper strata homes grew from `r round(100 * mix$strata_share[1])`% to `r round(100 * mix$strata_share[2])`% of sales, as in deck 05.

::: {.key-point}
The agent listed its choices. Reading them and acting on them is your job.
:::

## Check the row count after every join

```{r}
#| label: join-dup
sales <- tibble(sale_id = 1:3, neigh = c("Kitsilano", "West End", "Marpole"))
neigh_info <- tibble(neigh = c("Kitsilano", "Kitsilano", "West End", "Marpole"),
                     area_km2 = c(5.5, 5.5, 2.0, 5.8))

sales |> left_join(neigh_info, by = "neigh") |> nrow()
```

Three sales became four rows, because Kitsilano appears twice in `neigh_info`.

## Make R check the join for you

```{r}
#| label: join-relationship
sales |> left_join(neigh_info, by = "neigh", relationship = "many-to-one")
```

::: {.key-point}
`relationship = "many-to-one"` stops with an error if the right-hand table has duplicate keys.
:::

## A checklist for AI-written code

1. Read every line. Ask the AI to explain any line you cannot.
2. Count rows before and after each filter and join.
3. Look for missing values in every column you use, and count the rows they drop.
4. Compare magnitudes with a number you know. Is a median Vancouver house price of $200,000 plausible?
5. Plot the raw data before you summarise it.

## Let R write the numbers in your text

```{r}
#| label: van
van <- bca |> filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver")
```

````markdown
The data have `r knitr::inline_expr('format(nrow(van), big.mark = ",")')` sales in the City of Vancouver.
Their median price is `r knitr::inline_expr('format(median(van$price), big.mark = ",")')` dollars.
````

The report shows: The data have `r format(nrow(van), big.mark = ",")` sales in the City of Vancouver. Their median price is `r format(median(van$price), big.mark = ",")` dollars.

- A number you type stays the same after you or the AI change a filter or fix a join, and nothing warns you.
- Inline code runs again at every render. In PowerPoint, copy every number again from your final render.

::: {.key-point}
Every number in your text should come from R.
:::

## Work in small steps

1. For anything with more than one step, ask for a plan before any code.
2. Make one change at a time. Run it and check it before you go on.
3. Save a copy, or commit if you use Git, before an agent edits several files.
4. After two failed fixes, stop asking it to "try again". Restate the problem in a new conversation.

::: {.key-point}
Small steps keep every answer small enough to check.
:::

## Check a file you did not make

AI can write the import code. You check what it read, as in this made-up file:

```{r}
#| label: import-check
rents <- read_csv(I("area,units,median_rent
Burnaby,24510,\"1,725\"
Coquitlam,6875,1650
Lions Bay,12,**
Total,31397,1700"))
glimpse(rents)
```

What goes wrong if you sum `units`, or average `median_rent`?

## Three checks after any import

1. **Rows:** compare the count with the source, and look at the first and last rows for notes and totals. In `rents`, the `Total` row would double `sum(units)`.
2. **Types:** a number column read as `<chr>` hides symbols such as `**` (suppressed) or a comma, as in `median_rent`.
3. **One known number:** check that a total matches the published figure.

::: {.key-point}
AI coding agents can read your data files. Ask the agent to run these checks and show you the output.
:::

## Keep API keys out of AI conversations

- Keys live in `.Renviron`. Code reads them with `Sys.getenv()`.
- Never paste a key into a chat, your code, or a submission.
- A coding agent can open `.Renviron` like any file in `c407`. If a key appears in its output, treat the key as leaked.
- If a key leaks, delete it in the provider's console and create a new one.

## Say how you used AI

State the tool, what you used it for, and what you checked. For example:

::: {.small}
> I used [tool] to draft the code for Figures 2 and 3 and to fix a join error. I checked the row counts after each join and compared our totals with Statistics Canada's published figures.
:::

## Practice: find three mistakes

The task: compare the median price of single-family and strata homes in the City of Vancouver in 2025. This code runs without an error or a warning:

```{r}
#| label: practice-wrong
bca |>
  filter(aa_label == "Vancouver", year(sale_date) >= 2025) |>
  group_by(act_use_cat) |>
  summarise(median_price = mean(price), sales = n())
```

## Answer

```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: practice-answer
bca |>
  # 1. The City of Vancouver, not the wider assessment area
  # 2. 2025 only: 2026 is a partial year
  filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver", year(sale_date) == 2025) |>
  group_by(act_use_cat) |>
  # 3. median(), as the column name says
  summarise(median_price = median(price), sales = n())
```
